item.title: What can the animal rights movement learn from Dr. King?
item.description: Social Change = Vision + Values
item.content:encoded:
In the summer of 1963, Dr. King stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial and delivered what is perhaps the greatest speech in American history. With the usual boom in his voice, he confronted the nation’s conscience and delivered the famous words, “I Have A Dream.” Sixty years later, his speech is still just as iconic, and you’d be hard pressed to find someone who hasn’t heard of King’s vision for America. What made it so special?

Well, like most things, the Dream speech’s success probably comes down to the social context in which it was delivered. For example, before the March on Washington, King used several occasions to deliver versions of his Dream speech, but none of those occasions became particularly momentous. For that reason, one of his advisors warned against using the speech during the March on Washington because, “It’s trite, it’s cliche. You’ve used it too many times already.”1

Thanks for reading Ahimsa! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Fortunately, King’s advisor was wrong about that one. Perhaps because there’s something different about standing in front of 250,000 people during the climax of the civil rights movement.

Still, social context aside, there is something to be learned from the content of the Dream speech. And to me, that is most notably its positive vision. Dr. King’s dream was so beautifully vivid that he took everyone there with him. He spoke of the sons of slaveowners sitting down together with the sons of slaves; Black girls joining hands with White girls; and his four children, growing up in an America where they were no longer judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character.2 A world worth fighting for.

Perhaps even more importantly, Dr. King connected his vision to widely accepted American symbols. He spoke of the “great American” Abraham Lincoln, the “magnificent words” of the Constitution, and the good, old fashioned, “American dream.”

Similarly, King made absolutely sure to connect his vision with the most fundamental American value: freedom. In fact, King used the word “freedom” a whopping nineteen times in his Dream speech. And his final words were, “Free at last. Free at last. Thank God almighty, we are free at last.”

The combination of these two messaging tactics—painting a positive vision, and connecting it to widely held values—is a simple but brilliant formula for social change. I think the Dream speech owes much of its success to this combination.

Now, what can the animal rights movement learn from this example?

Well, when it comes to the first criteria of painting a positive vision, I feel like we’re miserably failing. Someone should actually study this, but my estimate is that something like 80 % of the online, animal rights content is negative. Negative in the sense that the content centers stuff like slaughterhouse footage, detailed descriptions of factory farming, messaging that implies that this is all your fault because you haven’t gone vegan yet… you get the point. Animal advocates are simply always talking about the problem.

I’m super guilty of this negative fixation myself. One look at my Instagram profile and just about every one of my animal-related posts has some sort of negative framing. I’m either talking about the “moral atrocity” of factory farming or the “tortured animals” on our plates. It actually feels exhausting for me to go through it all right now. I imagine it’s even worse for others.

The same goes for my in-person activism. I feel very comfortable riffing about the many ways in which animal agriculture is bad. But I struggle to speak for more than a few minutes about why the alternative is good. Heck, I don’t even have the clearest idea of what the alternative looks like!

Clearly, this is something for me, and the movement at large, to work on. Each of us should strive to articulate a positive vision in the way Dr. King was able to. And that vision should be communicated in a manner that is so undeniably just… so undeniably beautiful… that people can no longer resist joining in on our struggle.

And, I mean, this isn’t to say we should stop talking about the negative stuff. Indeed, we need to talk about the negative stuff, because who else is going to confront the world with the fact that our food system is one big fucking animal torture machine? Still, the animal torture machine can’t be all that we talk about. The gravity of this message is dreadful, overwhelming, and oftentimes charged with shame. That’s more than enough to make people turn away from us—or worse, turn against us. We need more of that “I Have A Dream” type energy to balance things out.

It’s also important to know our audience. I think negative content is probably best suited for the movement’s base supporters. Since these people already agree with us, negative messaging no longer carries the risk of alienation, and it also serves to channel the base’s outrage against the industry. For the general public, however, we probably need a stronger dose of positivity to make things more palatable.

What are some examples of positive content within the animal rights movement? Here are three of my favorites.

First, open rescue. Open rescue is a form of nonviolent direct action where activists remove animals from places of suffering and exploitation, usually a factory farm. By this act, an animal’s life is transformed from one of misery to one of joy.

Sanctuaries, where rescued animals are then taken, also play an important role in the rescue narrative. These are the magical places where rescued animals often touch grass for the first time, or cast their first glance up at the sky. Sanctuaries allow farmed animals to be centered as individuals, and provide them with a platform that, for once, is not undercover, graphic footage… but rather a joyful landscape, and a template of the world we can create.

The other positive messaging I’ve seen is Leah Garcés’ work with “transfarmations.” Through years of outreach and collaboration, Leah has persuaded over a dozen factory farmers to transition their animal farms to plant farms! These transfarmations are inspiring, concrete stories about the pathway to an alternative food system.

The last example of positive messaging I want to highlight is the artwork below. I love it so much because it perfectly contrasts the two alternatives. In one reality, we ship animals to their slaughter. And in the other, we feed them strawberries! Let’s feed pigs strawberries!

What I take from all three of these examples is that they all involve some form of transformation. I think this is a powerful framing for our movement—whether that involves slaughterhouses to sanctuaries, factory farmers to plant farmers, or cruelty to compassion. So yes, let’s have the courage to confront the ugliness of our reality. But let’s also have the imagination to envision the beauty of our alternative.

Now, onto step two: connecting the vision to widely held values. This is what Dr. King was going for when he very pointedly stated, “I still have a dream. It is a dream deeply rooted in the American dream.”

I feel like the animal rights movement is alright about doing this sort of thing. One of our best talking points on the matter is the classic refrain to household pets. We all love our pets… so why love one, but eat the other?

This question is an appeal to our shared value of kindness to animals. And it challenges us to reconsider the arbitrary categories that have been constructed around “food” and “companion” animals. After all, we all know it’s not kind to kill someone because you like the way they taste.

Another good way the movement appeals to public values is by putting factory farming on blast. Factory farming is cruel; factory farming is filthy; factory farming is unnatural. We need to keep drilling this message to make sure people understand: factory farming does not fit with our core values.

In particular, the best value for the animal rights movement to latch onto is probably human kindness. This is in contrast to the civil rights movement, which often set forth values like freedom and equality. Freedom and equality made a lot of sense for the civil rights movement, because Black people and other racial minorities were capable of becoming full members of society. The same, however, cannot be said of nonhuman animals. Due to this inherent vulnerability, I think it makes more sense for the animal rights movement to prioritize parental values like kindness, care, and guardianship. These values are more fitting given the nature of our relationship with nonhumans.3

I also like the “kindness” framing of animal rights, because it allows the human-nonhuman relationship to come into focus. I think this relational aspect is moving to people because, of course, we all want to be the kind stewards, not the violent overlords (the literal purpose of cognitive dissonance is to convince ourselves that this is so!). I fear the equality framing loses this relational aspect because, honestly, it centers the animals a little too much.

As for the movement’s greatest public relations weakness, alas… it’s probably the fact that we’re a bunch of vegans. This is a tough one, because people don’t like vegans. We’re perceived as annoying and preachy, countercultural and out-of-touch. That reduces our perceived credibility, and it makes it difficult for people to identify with our cause.

I think there are two main ways to remedy this. First, a significant portion of our movement has to go mainstream. That means scrapping all the edgy appearances. No more tattoos, piercings, or strange hairdos, and no more tie-dye, sandals, and mushrooms (I could work on this lol). We need to make ourselves less hippie, and more normie. Second, we need to decenter veganism and consumers, and recenter animals and systems. This second point deserves it’s own blog post, but the gist of what I mean here is that “go vegan” shouldn’t be our core talking point—it should just be a talking point. The central message should instead concern our damaged relationship with farmed animals, and the systemic change required to mend the relationship. This framing will create space for omnivores to align themselves with our cause, even if they are yet to fully align their actions.

Wrapping things up… any movement for social change should seek to (1) sketch the vision, and then (2) color in the values. For the animal rights movement, I think that means sketching a vision where our relationship to farmed animals is no longer one of violence, but one of kindness. I’m confident that if we work hard, and if we articulate this message with enough clarity and force, we will transform the world. Now let’s get to work!

1

The Guardian. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/aug/09/martin-luther-king-dream-speech-history

2

NPR. https://www.npr.org/2010/01/18/122701268/i-have-a-dream-speech-in-its-entirety

3

Of course, nonhuman animals are our equals. Accordingly, speciesism and the myth of human supremacy need to be dismantled. That being said, “equality for animals” is a tougher sell, and more confusing, than “kindness for animals.”

item.title: Rambling thoughts on my first Animal Law Conference
item.description: It was lit!
item.content:encoded:
It was lit! Hahaha nah I actually did really enjoy it though. There’s just something special about being in a room with hundreds of other people who are part of the same movement, fighting the same struggle.

I met professors who are making the legal arguments for animal personhood, movement lawyers who are defending activists, bureaucrats doing undergoing shit over at the Department of Agriculture, elected officials trying to leverage the power of the U.S. government, lobbyists fucking up the vivisection industry, and students—finding their way.

Thanks for reading Ahimsa! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

It really feels so special! Like networking shit is often so draining because you have to play the part and say the right things. But I didn’t really feel that way at all over at the conference. Like, we’re all here for the same reason you know. This movement is small and nobody’s here for the money (we don’t have any) or the clout (we also don’t have any). We’re here because we care about animals man!!!!! We care so fucking much!!!!!

Our community brought me so much joy for real. I want to hold onto that and spread it to the world.

I also stayed over with my friend T and it was so good reconnecting with her. She’s so sweet, and there was this one moment I had with her that I want to share with everyone just because it was so raw.

We were just chilling at her place, and talking about the age old difficulty of navigating a world where our loved ones are eating our loved ones. I shared about how my family eats animals with nearly every meal, and that’s especially true of my extended family. In particular, my little cousin goes crazy with it hahaha. It’s to the point that eating cows is literally part of his identity: everyone in the family knows steak is his favorite food, he loves to grill their flesh, and he literally has a fucking shirt about eating beef hahaha kms.

T heard that and she just started crying. Like actual tears—borderline sobs. “I don’t understand… I can’t believe children are wrapped up in this too… that cow was also someone’s baby… it’s not okay!”

I feel like I’m not capturing the moment too well but just trust me it was so raw. I wish I could capture her tears and pour them into my soul and your soul and everyone else’s too. That emotion will transform the world. I wish everyone could feel her sorrow because if they did it would move mountains.

Of course, I’m hopeful our movement will do that. We just have to be vulnerable, disciplined, organized. We need to capture the emotions we bleed, and spread them to every corner of the universe. The message will resonate. I know it with such certainty.

That leads me to the last point I wanted to make about the conference this weekend. My biggest critique is that the conference was lacking in vision and hope. Basically all of the panels were about making some marginal improvement to the system… which okay, yes, pragmatism requires us to consider marginal improvements... but at the very least, we should take care to connect marginal improvements with the grander vision of animal liberation—always keeping it within sight. I literally heard ZERO discussions—either on formal panels or interpersonally—about the pathway to factory farm abolition.

Why was nobody talking about this vision? Well, quite simply, I think it’s because most people do not believe in it. Most conference goers seemed to be of the opinion that the best we can possibly do is make marginal improvements.1

Take this conversation for example. I was talking with two senior activists who have been in the movement for decades. I asked what their biggest lesson for me was and they said, “Be realistic in your goals so you don’t burn yourself out. We’re never going to achieve animal liberation. We’re never going to end factory farming.” What the fuck??

I had the same conversation with like three other people. Me to an elected official, “I believe the animal rights movement could have a moment like BLM or Palestine within the next few years here. We have so much potential to transform the political landscape. And when we have that moment, elected officials like you will have way more wiggle room to advance pro-animal policies.” His response, “Sure… I hope you’re right.”

Me talking to an undergraduate student, “I’m hopeful we’ll end factory farming in our lifetimes!” His response, “I’m pessimistic.”

Me talking to T and her boyfriend, “People care about animals! We will change the world!” Her boyfriend’s response, “We’re never going to end factory farming. The industry is too powerful.”

Jesus fucking Christ. I feel so sorry for all of them. I feel like cynicism is a self-protective mechanism to prevent the soul crushing disappointment of living in a world where human society is still—no matter how hard we all seem to try—torturing our animal friends in mass. And I mean, I get it. The fact that human society is willing to tolerate an atrocity of these proportions is mind boggling indeed. It makes it way too easy to think that “nobody cares” and “humanity is evil” are the only explanations for the problem’s persistence.

But those aren’t the only explanations. People do care, and I see it everywhere. It’s in the insistence that “I only eat humane meat.” It’s in the aversion to watching animals suffer. It’s in the love we have for stuffed animals, baby animals, companion animals. Indeed, we are a compassionate species! We just need to design the social structures to unleash that compassion.

Anyway, our movement’s cynicism is a huge problem. What are we doing at the animal law conference if not seriously discussing the pathway to animal liberation? We need to be more ambitious. Dream people!! Dr. King didn’t persuade people because he wanted to sit closer to the front of the bus; he said EQUALITY BITCH. GIVE ME EQUALITY.

The animal rights movement needs to bring that same energy. Dreaming of factory farms with slightly *less torturous* practices is not a particularly inspiring vision. Nah, shut that shit the fuck down! I want every bird out of their cage and into the sky.

This is a gap for all of us to fill. Collectively, we need to set clear and ambitious goals. And collectively, we need to fill our minds with clarity, and our hearts with hope.

Together, we can do it. I promise.

1

I think perhaps the animal law conference was disproportionately pessimistic relative to the greater movement because lawyers tend to be conservative, inside-the-system thinkers. But the greater movement could use a strong dose of vision and hope too.

item.title: Animal Rights: At a Polling Station Near You!
item.description: Two ballot initiatives launch animal rights into the political mainstream
item.content:encoded:
I’m voting for Kamala. But honestly, I don’t care that much about her election. The deeper I get into the animal rights movement, the more I feel like the pro-Palestine people who are like, “Democrats? Republicans? It’s genocide all the same!” The same is true of animal issues. Both parties overwhelmingly support the mass slaughter of nonhumans. It’s hard to feel too invested in that arrangement.

Fortunately, even for disaffected, pro-animal voters such as myself, there is reason to care about this year’s election. Later today, we’ll receive the results from the two most ambitious, pro-animal ballot initiatives in American history. One of them, Measure J in Sonoma County, California, would shut down or downsize over twenty factory farms. The other, Prop 309 in Denver, Colorado, would shutter the doors of the largest industrial lamb slaughterhouse in the nation. Local voters will control these outcomes—for once, not with their dietary choices—but rather by checking a box at the polls. What will they choose?

Thanks for reading Ahimsa! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The optimistic theory for these ballot initiatives rests on the distinction between individual and collective action. On an individual level, for example, most people are reluctant to stop eating animals.1 But on a collective level, so the theory goes, more people are willing to transition our food system away from its abuse of animals. Thus, ballot initiatives are perfectly suited for this problem, as they transform animal rights from an individual, consumer choice (vegetarianism) into a collective, political one (slaughterhouse ban).2

More than a few times, the animal rights movement has received evidence to support this theory. Take California’s Prop 12 for example. Prior to Prop 12, which banned the egg industry’s use of battery cages, only about 14 % of Californians went out of their way to purchase cage-free eggs. Does that mean only 14 % of Californians supported Prop 12’s ban on cages? Far from it! Californians voted overwhelmingly in support of the hens—a whopping 62 % in favor!

Now the question is, will this “personally no, collectively yes” theory hold true for Measure J and Prop 309’s more ambitious attempts to ban factory farms and slaughterhouses? Unfortunately, my prediction is no—I expect both initiatives to fail (I’ll save the subject of why for another post).

Regardless of these outcomes, however, the ballot initiatives still give me enormous hope for our movement’s future. How could impending failure be so inspiring, you might ask? Well, let’s take a dive deeper into the initiative I’ve most directly been part of.

Measure J — Sonoma County, California

The first time I went door knocking for Measure J was in June, relatively early in the campaign season. Almost none of the voters I talked to that day had heard of the initiative, and literally everyone was supportive. “Factory farms? Oh no, we don’t like those. We’ll vote Yes on J.”

Since then, the vibes in Sonoma County have switched up quite dramatically. The last time I went door knocking in mid-September, almost everyone had already heard of Measure J, and almost everyone was decided against it. “Sorry, I’m No on J. I support our local farms.” What happened between June and September?

To put it simply, the factory farm industry organized itself, and quite effectively at that. For the last few months, Measure J has arguably been the most polarizing issue in all of Sonoma. The local papers provide near continuous Measure J coverage; “No on J” yard signs are strewn all along the county, particularly within its agricultural districts; and various industry groups have spent record amounts—more than a million dollars—to defeat what would typically be a lowly funded, county initiative.

And the industry did more than just organize itself, it also brought together the local Democratic and Republican parties! In this beautiful act of bipartisanship, two unlikely bedfellows reconciled their differences to defend one of our nation’s most sacred values: torturing the fuck out of animals before eating them.

Witnessing the vibe shift against Measure J has been disheartening. What initially felt like a winnable, transformative campaign, now looks more like a modest “conversation starter.” Of course, someone has to start the conversation… but I can’t help but wish things were as simple as the first time I went door knocking.

Unfortunately, change is not that simple. As with all social movements, our cause’s moral righteousness will become self-evident… in hindsight. In the heat of the moment, however, there will always “more to the story,” and our movement has no choice but to wade through the opposition’s various denials, deflections, and rationalizations.

It is the very the nature of these rationalizations, however, that give me cause for hope. Let’s briefly examine them:

(1) Measure J hurts farmers. Farmers shouldn’t have to shut down their farms. Many of these farms are family owned, and some of them have been in Sonoma for generations.

(2) Measure J hurts taxpayers. Transitioning away from factory farming will impose costs on taxpayers. These costs will be included in the price of animal products, as well as the price of retraining workers.

(3) Measure J eliminates jobs. Everyone working at a factory farm will lose their job, and the same goes for some third-party suppliers.

(4) Measure J doesn’t help animals. Since California passed Prop 12, and since third-party certifiers verify animal welfare standards, the animals are already doing fine.

(5) Measure J is run by outsider, vegan extremists. Don’t let these people dictate how we operate.

So, these are the arguments at the core of the opposition’s messaging. What do you notice about them?

What stands out to me is that none of these arguments even attempt to argue with the premise of Measure J. They either distract from the animal welfare concerns at the heart of the issue. Or, when they do address animal welfare, they just straight up lie about it.3 “Everything’s fine!” they say. Does this look fine to you?

I’m confident that this two-prong strategy of “deflect and deny” will prove unsustainable for the factory farm industry. No on J may win today at the ballot box, but over the coming decades, the factory farm industry will crumble. This is apparent from the industry’s inability to reckon with the horror at the heart of its operations. No on J makes zero attempt to justify the cruelty, the crowding, or the cannibalism, because it knows all too well that these are losing arguments. People do not want animals to be tortured. Thus, the industry’s sole defense mechanisms include (1) erasing the victims from the conversation, or (2) outright lying about how they are treated.

This is the factory farm industry’s most damning fact: the American people care about animals. Indeed, I observed this concern every day as I canvassed the streets of Sonoma; not a single person was pleased to see images like the one above. “Oh, please don’t show me those photos,” was one of the most common refrains.

This discomfort with factory farming is rooted in a deep compassion for our fellow creatures. We care for them so much, that we are literally unable to tolerate the sight of their suffering. Thus, our job as animal advocates is not to instill pro-animal values, but rather to unleash them. Ballot initiatives like Measure J are worthy attempts at this pursuit, but, as I expect we’ll learn later today, there is still work to do.

1

For decades, Gallup has found that the percentage of Americans who identify as vegetarian has remained stagnant at around 5 %.

2

Ballot initiatives also conveniently sidestep the legislature, giving the decision directly to the people. This is helpful for animal issues, because the legislature is fully in bed with the industry.

3

Take these FAQs straight from the No on J website. One of the answers literally has the nerve to say, “animals are given the ability to move around freely, even in an operation considered a CAFO [factory farm].” That’s fucking wild.

item.title: What should we celebrate?
item.description: Reflections on passing the bar exam
item.content:encoded:
A week ago, I passed the California bar exam! I’m proud of myself for that. I worked hard to get here, and I will work hard to use this credential to help others. Still, I have mixed feelings about all the celebrations.

For context, passing the bar exam is a big deal for all of us law students! After the results dropped, everyone was up on social media posting about their passing scores, and my friends and I have been exchanging congratulations for the last week. The same goes for my family. Everyone, my extended family included, was texting and calling to celebrate me passing this milestone. That all creates for a heavy culture of celebration.

Thanks for reading Ahimsa! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

I’m of two minds about this. On the one hand, I’m super happy and appreciative. My classmates and I worked hard, and I’m grateful to have others acknowledge that. Indeed, we should drink to our accomplishments!

On the other hand, I’m salty and annoyed. Like, why are we all doing the most to celebrate something that feels so self-centered? Becoming a lawyer has almost no correlation with helping others or making the world a better place. It’s more just a hoop that we’re jumping through—a really shiny, expensive hoop that adorns us with earning potential and social status.1

That’s especially true of my friends who are going into Big Law. They will become the legal sidearm of corporate America, ensuring that the system continues to serve the rich and powerful. That feels more like something to lament, not celebrate.

For my public interest friends, at least we’re doing something to help the world. But even then, that’s not really what we’re celebrating with this bar exam. We’re celebrating our newfound lawyerdom, not the altruistic careers we’re pursuing.

Of course, we should take moments to celebrate our accomplishments, even if those accomplishments are totally divorced from any notion of “doing good.” I just think it becomes problematic when our celebration of selfish accomplishments, such as passing the bar exam, does so much to outshine our celebration of altruistic accomplishments, such as pursuing the public interest. This sends a signal to society that we value behaviors that are associated with money and prestige, not behaviors that are associated with service and care. In turn, that creates a backwards system of social incentives, where people are encouraged to behave in their own self interest more than they are encouraged to serve the community.

Let’s call this the “celebration gap”: the gap between the celebration of selfish accomplishments and the celebration of altruistic accomplishments. The disproportionate celebration of selfish accomplishments implicitly creates a hierarchy of achievement—one where people pursuing the top of the hierarchy do absolutely nothing to help anyone, or worse, actively harm others along the way.

This celebration gap was more than present at Berkeley Law. For example, the three most celebrated accomplishments were probably good grades, Big Law job offers, and judicial clerkships. None of those accomplishments really have anything to do with improving the state of the world.2 More than anything, they’re about money and clout. We should be celebrating things like political advocacy, direct services, and nonprofit work instead.

The celebration gap also extends beyond Berkeley Law and into greater society. The most obvious example of this is attaining wealth. We’re literally always celebrating people for getting rich, and that’s so dumb! In a world of outstanding poverty, wealth hoarding is shameful and immoral. Please give your money to poor people instead.

Admittedly, a lot of my saltiness around this “celebration gap” is coming from my personal experience. Over the last few years, I’ve put so much time and energy into helping animals. Their suffering is my labor, my thought, my emotion. This is the work I’m truly proud of, and yet, I’ve received far less kudos for it than I have passing the bar exam! That actually makes me so upset. Here I am, pouring my heart into what is one of the darkest tragedies of the modern era… but few people seem to recognize it. Instead, they just want to congratulate me for passing this damn test!

We really need to redesign this state of affairs. How can we reconfigure our social norms and institutions such that the celebration gap is skewed in the opposite direction? That way, people who are tempted to climb the hierarchy of achievement will be acting in the public interest by default. Just imagine if all the gunners who did the most in law school directed their energy towards something like animal advocacy instead.

Flipping the celebration gap is a difficult project that I don’t have all the answers to. But, as a simple place to start, let’s do more to celebrate the people in our lives who dedicate themselves to the community. And maybe… every once in a while… let’s also shit on our classmates who go into Big Law.

1

I know it’s easier for me to call lawyerdom a “hoop” given my background. I’m super privileged, and my dad is already a lawyer. In that way, it’s way less hype for me to attain attorney status than some of my other friends who actually beat the odds to get here.

2

It’s possible to leverage accomplishments like good grades, big law jobs offers, and judicial clerkships into something that helps others. But as these systems are designed, I don’t think any of these accomplishments are directly aligned with the public interest.

item.title: Luigi Mangione, Blackpilling, and the Future of Animal Rights
item.description: Last Monday at 3:45pm, Luigi Mangione made his way into my world by means of a Partiful comment.
item.content:encoded:
Last Monday at 3:45pm, Luigi Mangione made his way into my world by means of a Partiful comment. The comment read, “Did you guys see how hot the united healthcare ceo killer is…?" To which someone responded, “Luigi 🤤.”

Since then, it seems that just about everyone is discussing Luigi’s assassination of UnitedHealthCare's CEO, Brian Thompson. My roommate texted me to ask whether I support the assassination of factory farm CEOs (I don’t), and my friend group casually discussed who the next best assassination target would be (perhaps another healthcare CEO, or maybe someone from the equally evil, pharmaceutical industry). On a national level, there has been endless social media attention, political analysis, and multiple, Luigi Mangione look alike competitions. Please allow me to add to the discourse.

My basic take is that Luigi Mangione is “blackpilled”—or disillusioned—with the state of the world, and this blackpilling is a larger cultural trend which the animal rights movement must reckon with and seize upon. This includes adaptations to our messaging strategy, as well as more investment in grassroots organizing and nonviolent direct action.

Subscribe now

Taking a step back now, what exactly does it mean to be “blackpilled?” And how do we know Luigi swallowed the pill?

The black pill is a metaphor that first emerged on the online manosphere. Adapted from the Matrix’s “red pill”—which awakens its protagonist to a previously hidden reality—the black pill awakens incels to the reality that their lowly social status is predetermined by inferior genetics, destining them to a life of loneliness and marginalization. This realization leaves the blackpilled incel with two options: (1) reveling in their misery, or (2) enacting mass violence to create systemic change.1

Blackpilling has now expanded beyond these depressing incel forums and into more mainstream discourse. The word’s central meaning, however, stays true to its incel etymology. It is used to communicate a deep pessimism about the state of the world. An “everything’s fucked, nothing matters,” type of energy.

Blackpilling is a very useful term to describe the state of the world today. In my own social networks, I feel as if I’m one of the few people who’s genuinely hopeful about our collective future, and this tracks with national trends. 46 % of Gen-Z thinks humanity is doomed;2 Americans are more lonely than ever;3 and the public’s trust in nearly every social institution including Congress, criminal justice, media, healthcare, public schools, and organized religion, is at an all time low.4 By murdering Brian Thompson, Luigi unleashed these blackpilled sentiments and put them on full display. Sympathy for someone’s murder? No, try a self-satisfied, sarcastic glee instead.

Luigi’s own worldview is a product of this widespread, American blackpilling. He’s not a member of the far left or the far right, and he’s not an incel or a white supremacist. No, Luigi is far more normal than any of that: he’s someone who lost faith in America. This is most evident in his determination that the healthcare system was bleak enough to require murder. (Read his alleged manifesto, “These [indecipherable] have simply gotten too powerful, and they continue to abuse our country for immense profit… I am the first to face it with such brutal honesty.”)5 Likewise, Luigi’s social media presence, although somewhat scattered, can generally be defined by a distrustful, anti-establishment sentiment.6

Most fascinating to me is Luigi’s apparent interest in my supervisor at work, Wayne Hsiung. (Wayne is one of the animal rights movement’s most prominent figures, and he is best known for organizing civil disobedience, typically in the form of rescuing animals from factory farms. Consequently, Wayne has been convicted of multiple felonies and sentenced to time behind bars.)7 Luigi only follows 71 people on X, but Wayne is one of them! Even better, Luigi retweeted the verdict from one of Wayne’s criminal trials, where he was prosecuted for rescuing two piglets from a factory farm.8

Now, why exactly did this radical and somewhat fringe animal rights activist—one with a following of less than 10k on X—appeal to someone like Luigi? I’d like to believe that it’s because Luigi was a closeted vegan… one with deep commitments to animal liberation. But more likely, the explanation has its roots in the same distrust and anti-establishment sentiment that motivated Luigi’s act of murder. Like Luigi, Wayne has also sacrificed his freedoms to oppose one of the most deceitful, heartless, and gargantuan industries in all of America: animal agriculture. Clearly, that is something Luigi can resonate with.

The most apparent difference between Wayne and Luigi, however, is in their tactics. While Luigi resorted to first-degree murder, Wayne is a strict adherent to nonviolence, and will not even engage in property damage. Nonetheless, Wayne’s peace sign, pacifistic style of activism was successful in attracting a proponent of political violence like Luigi. What can the animal rights movement learn from this?

I take two main lessons. First, the animal rights movement should do even more to prioritize the framing of animal agriculture as a deceitful and untrustworthy industry. We already do this a lot (unfortunately, the industry gives us plenty to work with), but I think we should go even harder. I want every single American to understand how much the industry is bullshitting everyone. 99 % of farmed animals reside on factory farms!9 99 % ! That means that despite all of the industry’s attempts to humanewash its products with labels like “humane,” “free range,” “organic,” and “pasture raised,” nearly every strip of meat came from an animal who was confined and tortured.10 The images of happy animals on rolling hills are such a sham that it’s almost funny.

This “deceitful industry” framing will resonate with the growing demographic of distrustful Americans like Luigi. Since the blackpilled are already primed to believe that corporations are lying to them, it shouldn’t take much to explain that the animal agriculture industry is doing it too. Within a matter of years, we should aim for the animal agriculture industry to adopt the same public reputation as the healthcare industry: evil, corrupt, untrustworthy.

My second takeaway from this Luigi // Wayne crossover is that the animal rights movement needs to invest more in grassroots organizing and direct action. Wayne didn’t appeal to Luigi by putting his head down and working within the establishment. That sort of “inside game” advocacy would never have resonated with Luigi because Luigi, like many Americans, had already lost all faith in the system. Thus, Luigi was unlikely to be inspired by traditional forms of advocacy like electoral campaigns, ballot initiatives, or lobbying efforts. Institutional activism is simply unable to inspire those who don’t believe in our institutions… for the blackpilled among us, something different is needed.

I believe that something is the twofold strategy of community organizing and nonviolent direct action. Only these strategies are capable of restoring the sense of hope and agency that every social movement requires. Community is the battery to store our collective hope and resilience; direct action is the catalyst to its expression.

In a world of increasing pessimism and isolation, we need one another to stave off the impending sense of doom. Few of us are strong enough to remain committed in the face of a crowd who screams, “Nothing will change. Your efforts are futile.” Together, however, we can form a protective shield around the vision of the world we want to create. Reinforcing, echoing, and amplifying the hope in our hearts.

Direct action transforms this hope into something tangible and undeniable. It allows people to take power back into their own hands, and it communicates to our blackpilled brothers and sisters, “I know the system is broken, but there is another way.” Together, we will walk directly into these factories of violence, and together, we will walk out with the animals in our arms. We will show them the love they have never experienced but always deserved; and we will not stop until our message is stricken into the soul of our nation.

This resolve to take matters into our own hands—to go out and fix what everyone already knows to be broken—is why I believe Luigi Mangione was drawn to Wayne Hsiung. Unfortunately, however, even Luigi’s faith in nonviolent direct action seems to have been shattered. That is, of course, why he resorted to shooting Brian Thompson through the head.

The despair that drove Luigi to such desperate measures is a problem that our society—and every serious social movement—must reckon with. If we are to prevent further descent into polarization and political violence, we must provide people a viable alternative. Given the growing distrust in American institutions, that alternative is unlikely to take the form of conventional politics; we need something more communal, more participatory, and more inspiring.

For the environmental movement, perhaps that is planting trees on the sites of fossil fuel extraction. For the healthcare movement, perhaps that is organizing free healthcare clinics within insurance company headquarters. And, for the animal rights movement, that is rescuing animals from the bloodstained floors where they are taken to be killed, and carrying them to sanctuaries of comfort and love. This juxtaposition of imagery—light shining amidst a shroud of darkness—has the power to inspire the masses, and transform our world. Let us shine the light!

item.title: Holy shit... the legal system might actually do something to help animals 🤯
item.description: Animal law was once described to me as trying to fit a round peg into a square hole.
item.content:encoded:
Animal law was once described to me as trying to fit a round peg into a square hole. Fair enough. With few legal protections for animals—and a legal system that is reluctant to enforce them—animal lawyers are often forced to get “creative” with their arguments. Indeed, that is the only way to fit a round peg into a square hole. Creatively.1

While this practice has created some change on the margins, altogether, it has failed to stop the animal exploitation machine. In large part, this is due to industry capture of our government institutions. Legislatures create exemptions for institutionalized animal abuse;2 prosecutors refuse to prosecute industry violations;3 and courts are reluctant to disrupt the status quo.

Given this state of affairs, our court decision from last week is astounding. The judge in our nonprofit’s case against Ridglan Farms—an industrial facility that breeds thousands of dogs for cruel and invasive experiments—approved our petition to appoint a “special prosecutor.”4 That means, for one of the first times in America, a government official will be appointed to prosecute an industrial animal abuser. If the prosecution succeeds, the over 3,000 dogs confined to Ridglan Farms may be freed from their cages and placed in loving homes.

For context, Ridglan Farms is a literal hellscape for our canine friends. I’ve met one of the dogs rescued from this facility, Julie, and she remains traumatized from her stay there. Seven years later, she still struggles to go on walks, and she maintains her habit of repeatedly spinning in circles—always clockwise, turning over her right shoulder. The endless spinning is a behavior she developed at Ridglan Farms, as circling was her only recourse from madness.

See the video below. Julie is the dog at the bottom.

Thankfully, later this same day, Julie’s spinning was interrupted by a pair of loving arms—arms that carried her out of this wretched facility, and into the loving home of my friend Diana. Today, Julie and Diana spend most of their hours side by side. Diana tells me that, although Julie will never be a normal dog, she is generally happy and affectionate.

Unfortunately, there are still thousands of dogs spinning inside Ridglan Farms. They are subject to intensive confinement, wired floors that cut their feet, and cruel, invasive surgeries. Above all, they are lonely—wholly deprived of the human companionship that all dogs crave.

Much of this information was obtained by my friend Scotty, who worked undercover at the facility back in 2022. I have no idea how he managed, but somehow he did. Perhaps the darkest, most evil scientist-ish story revealed by him and another whistleblower concerns what are called “devocalization surgeries.” To cope with the deafening barks generated by thousands of trapped, rabid dogs, Ridglan Farms literally severs dogs’ vocal cords. This entails drugging a dog to paralyze him, prying open his mouth, holding it open using a special contraption, reaching down his throat with a razor, and then slicing the cords in the back of his throat. This is all performed without anesthesia.5

Making matters worse is the vivisection industry’s preferred breed of test subjects: beagles. Nearly all experimented dogs are beagles, and that is because they are the most gentle and docile of breeds. You can abuse them relentlessly, but they will still love you.6

The atrocities unfolding at Ridglan Farms are infuriating enough just to write about. Fortunately, our judge has provided the movement an opportunity to rescue these dogs and shut down the facility once and for all. And, once Ridglan Farms falls, the vivisection industry will have just one remaining, industrial dog breeder in America.7 This is, hopefully, the beginning of the end for all companion animal testing. Let’s make it happen.

What is to be learned from this (hopefully, soon-to-be) victory? I take two main lessons.

First, the law is lagging. There is a reason that our case involving dogs has received court approval, but not our case involving pigs. In fact, none of our farmed animal cases have gotten anywhere close to inducing the prosecution of a factory farm—Ridglan’s agricultural equivalent. This discrepancy is the product of speciesism: we love dogs, but we eat pigs. Thus, the court system—a conservative, government institution—is, predictably, more comfortable defending companion animals than farmed animals. Indeed, our judge understands that backing her up is not just the feeble, animal rights movement, but also the combined force of America’s humane societies and dog moms. The weight of this public opinion has empowered her to take a stand against the vivisection industry.

That is why I say the law is lagging. While pro-dog sentiments have existed for decades, it is only now that the government is beginning to transform this sentiment into policy. Using the round peg // square hole analogy from earlier, public opinion has performed the vital work of rounding out the square hole, making courtroom victory a possibility for our canine companions.

I fear that when it comes to farmed animals, the greater animal law movement is stuck with the round peg in its hand, banging tirelessly at a square hole that will never budge. Given our current social context, it is doubtful that even the most skilled of animal lawyers could convince a judge to shut down a factory farm. That is because legal arguments do not convince judges to upend the status quo. Judges are just like everyone else… they only go out on a limb when they feel supported by a larger group, and when they feel like the tides are shifting.

The animal rights movement must create these social conditions by winning the battle of public opinion. This begins by acknowledging that the vast majority of the public opinion “playing field” exists outside the courtroom. The battle will be waged on the streets, in classrooms, and on media platforms. Not courtrooms. (Courtrooms may play some role in the public opinion battle, but only if they are tied to a greater movement strategy. Isolated court cases—even those with the most meritorious and creative of arguments—are of limited value until the broader social context has been shifted.)

So, enough with the narrow-minded, litigation strategy. We are not going to litigate the animals to liberation. No, we need a social movement to attack speciesism on all fronts. Accordingly, the purpose of the animal law sphere should be to support our movement’s activists… to provide them the legal cover they need to hack away at the stubborn, sharp edges constituting our legal system’s square hole. Then, once society has been sufficiently provoked—and public opinion sufficiently shifted—our lawyers may finally use the round pegs they have so desperately been waiting to use.8

Finally, my second takeaway from the Ridglan Farms victory is that government institutions can be rewired. This is already obvious when we look to history (e.g., a government that once upheld slavery is now committed to its abolition). But it is even more heartening to see this switch up in real time. Just a year ago, the court system now prosecuting Ridglan Farms was previously prosecuting animal activists. Their crime? Rescuing dogs from Ridglan Farms. Oh how the turns have tabled.

This same reversal can—and will—be accomplished at scale. Within our lifetimes, the very United States government that once upheld the animal exploitation machine will work to dismantle it. Ridglan Farms and its animal abusing associates will become the villains of history, and our relationship to these gentle creatures will be transformed. No longer one of violence, but one of kindness.

What’s up this week?

  • Meetup! Tomorrow, Scotty, Diana, and I will be on a panel at the DxE meetup to discuss all of this in more detail. Join us at 11am at the Animal Rights Center for good vibes and vegan brunch!

  • Donald Trump. On Monday, President Trump will be inaugurated once more. Our nonprofit, the Animal Rescue Coalition, is hosting a summit in Washington D.C. during the weekend of March 14th to respond to these events. This summit will be an opportunity to make national headlines, and to shift the course of decades of government ag policy. I’ll speak more on this soon, but for now, check out our Eventbrite for more info.

2
